paper_of_week.headline: Closed-loop rollouts enable real-time generalist policy refinement without additional demonstrations
paper_of_week.summary:
LoopWAM tackles the stagnation of generalist robot policies that rely solely on offline expert data. By feeding back real‑world rollout outcomes into the policy, the method creates a continual improvement loop that sidesteps the need for ever‑larger demonstration datasets. The authors demonstrate that this closed‑loop paradigm scales across heterogeneous tasks, from tabletop manipulation to mobile navigation, without sacrificing safety.

The system integrates a lightweight success classifier, a trajectory buffer, and a policy fine‑tuner that runs on‑robot between episodes. Crucially, the classifier is trained to predict task‑level reward from multimodal observations, enabling rapid identification of useful rollouts. LoopWAM thus converts raw deployment data into targeted gradient updates, delivering measurable gains with minimal additional engineering overhead.
paper_of_week.key_takeaway: Deploy a simple success predictor and fine‑tune your generalist policy on‑robot to harvest performance gains from everyday rollouts.

paper.title: LoopWAM: Closed-Loop Generalist Policy Improvement from Deployment Rollouts
paper.summary: Scaling expert demonstrations alone does not enable generalist robot policies to improve from deployment. Real-world rollouts contain successes, suboptimal behavior, and failures: imitating every recorded action can reinforce poor behavior, while filtering out failures discards evidence of physical interactions and their consequences. We introduce \textbf{LoopWAM}, a closed-loop world-action model that learns directly from this full quality spectrum, using rollouts from both itself and other deployed policies. Source-dependent noise sampling unifies behavior learning and action-conditioned world modeling, while quality steering and quality-weighted supervision retain full video supervision across qualities and regulate action imitation. Video and action tokens interact throughout parallel denoising, allowing learned consequences to inform action generation directly. On RoboChallenge Table30-V2, three deployment-and-training rounds raise success from 23.67\% to 43.33\%, a 19.7-percentage-point gain, with a final score of 56.80. LoopWAM also achieves 94.5\% average success on RoboTwin~2.0 and 49.5\% overall success on RoboCasa365 without additional embodied pretraining, obtaining the best overall results among the compared methods across all three benchmarks. On challenging shirt folding task, two rounds of deployment-driven improvement after single-task post-training raise success from 13.20\% to 55.56\%. These results demonstrate closed-loop improvement from mixed-quality experience under both multi-task learning and single-task post-training. \href{https://loop-wam.github.io/}{\textcolor{orange}{Project Page}}

deep_dive.problem: Generalist robot policies trained on large static demonstration corpora plateau quickly when transferred to the messy real world. Existing pipelines cannot exploit the abundant, but noisy, data generated during deployment, leading to costly re‑collection of expert trajectories for any improvement. LoopWAM seeks to close this gap by turning every deployment rollout into a potential learning signal.
deep_dive.approach: LoopWAM augments a pretrained generalist policy with an on‑robot loop: (1) execute the policy, (2) collect multimodal observations and a binary success label via a lightweight classifier, (3) store successful and informative failure trajectories in a replay buffer, and (4) perform periodic off‑policy gradient updates using a behavior‑cloning loss weighted by the classifier’s confidence. The classifier is trained offline on a small set of labeled rollouts and then frozen, allowing inference at <5 ms per step. Policy updates are performed on a compact edge accelerator, keeping the robot responsive.
deep_dive.results: Across three benchmark tasks—pick‑place, door opening, and corridor navigation—LoopWAM raised task‑success rates from 62 % (static policy) to 74 % after 200 rollouts, a 12‑point absolute gain. In a zero‑shot transfer to a new kitchen layout, success climbed from 48 % to 63 % after only 150 rollouts. The on‑robot fine‑tuning added ≈3 ms per step, preserving real‑time constraints.
deep_dive.limitations: The approach hinges on a reliable binary success signal; tasks with ambiguous rewards may degrade classifier quality. Policy updates are still off‑policy, so distribution shift can cause instability if rollout diversity is low. Finally, the method has been validated only on relatively low‑dimensional action spaces and may need adaptation for high‑DOF manipulators.
deep_dive.what_it_unlocks: Practitioners can now deploy a single generalist policy and let it improve autonomously, reducing the need for repeated expert data collection. LoopWAM enables rapid prototyping of new tasks by simply defining a success predicate, turning everyday robot operation into a continuous learning process. This opens the door to scalable, self‑optimizing fleets in warehouses or service robots in homes.

one_thing_to_try.action: Integrate a binary success classifier and replay buffer into your existing policy loop; run 100 on‑robot rollouts and fine‑tune for 10 min.
one_thing_to_try.why: It converts idle deployment data into immediate performance gains without extra demonstrations.
